screens.title: Introduction to C# and Visual Studio for Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn how C# scripts plug into Unity, why Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code is the recommended editor, and how the MonoBehaviour lifecycle drives script execution. We'll walk through configuring your external script editor inside Unity preferences so you gain features like code completion and debugging. Then you'll open a generated script, identify the using directives, class declaration, and example lifecycle methods. You'll add a simple public variable so it shows in the Inspector, attach the script to a 3D object, and press Play to confirm Awake and Start messages appear in the Console. This foundation matters because it turns static scenes into interactive behaviors and gives you the tools to inspect and fix runtime problems quickly. A common misconception is that a script automatically runs without being attached; it must be a component on a GameObject to trigger lifecycle callbacks. As you progress, these basics will let you prototype movement, interactions, and game state reliably. Keep an eye on the Console for Debug. Log messages; they are your first diagnostics. Ready to start exploring the topics and step-by-step exercises that follow?

Set up your editor, open a new script, and watch Unity call lifecycle methods when the scene runs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure Unity to use Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code as the external C# editor, create and inspect a basic C# script, and attach it to a GameObject so it executes. You will understand the main syntax elements: using directives, class declarations, variables with explicit data types, and comments. You will be able to expose public variables to the Inspector for rapid tuning and use the Console to observe Debug. Log output. Finally, you'll know when to use Awake versus Start for initialization and how that affects dependencies between objects. Each objective links practical steps to why they matter: editor configuration unlocks IntelliSense and debugging which speeds development; knowing script structure prevents common attachment mistakes; and correctly timed initialization prevents race conditions between objects. These skills let you move from static scenes to interactive prototypes quickly, and they form the foundation for movement, input handling, and component interactions you'll learn next.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Checks
screens.narratorSegment: This screen expands the objectives into verifiable steps you can perform. You'll create a project and a simple script, attach it to a 3D object, and confirm Console output from both Awake and Start. You will also edit a public variable, change it in the Inspector, and run again to see the updated value printed. These checks are important because they prove both script attachment and Inspector exposure are working. We'll also highlight common pitfalls, such as forgetting to attach the script, disabling the component, or mis-typing a variable so its default value does not appear. Completing these actions gives you a short checklist to move forward with movement, input, and more advanced scripting patterns.

screens.title: Configure Visual Studio as Unity's External Script Editor
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Unity to use Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code as the external script editor is a small step that yields big productivity gains. Begin by opening Unity, then open Edit, Preferences, and the External Tools section. There you will select Visual Studio or V S Code as the External Script Editor. This connection gives you code completion, symbol lookup, and the ability to attach the debugger to a running Unity editor. A concrete example: when you open a C# script from the Project window, Visual Studio will show method suggestions and automatically jump to definitions, which saves time versus searching manually. A common misconception is that any editor will behave the same with Unity; in practice, the integrated tooling the IDE provides is the difference between slow trial-and-error and fast iterative debugging. If your scripts don't open in the selected editor, check the package installation and confirm Unity was restarted after installing Visual Studio components. Finally, test your setup by creating a simple script, opening it, and verifying that IntelliSense suggests types like GameObject and MonoBehaviour and that breakpoints hit when you attach the debugger. This verification closes the loop and ensures your development environment is ready for rapid scripting.

screens.title: Anatomy of a New C# Script
screens.narratorSegment: A freshly created C# script in Unity follows a predictable skeleton that helps Unity wire your code into the engine. At the top you will see using directives. These are short statements that allow your code to reference namespaces that contain types and utilities. For Unity development, UnityEngine is the essential namespace because it holds GameObject, Transform, and many engine services. Below that you find a class declaration. The typical form declares a public class that inherits from MonoBehaviour. Inheritance from MonoBehaviour is what enables the script to be attached to a GameObject as a component and to receive lifecycle callbacks from Unity. Inside the class you will initially see methods like Start and Update. Start runs once before the first frame update if the component is enabled, and Update runs every frame. Many learners assume methods in a script run automatically even if the script is not attached; that is a misconception. A class that does not inherit from MonoBehaviour cannot be added as a component. A concrete example is creating PlayerController : MonoBehaviour and observing that after you attach it to a Cube, the Start method runs and prints a message. Understanding this structure prevents common errors and sets you up to add variables and behaviors safely.

keyIdea.title: Script Skeleton
keyIdea.text: using directives import namespaces; the public class inherits MonoBehaviour so the script can attach to GameObjects and receive lifecycle callbacks.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Script Anatomy
Core Concept

Script skeleton explained

using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    void Start()
    {
        // called before the first frame update
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // called once per frame
    }
}
using directives let you reference engine types. The class line declares a component you can attach. Start and Update are lifecycle hooks Unity calls at predictable times.
Misconception: code runs by being present. Reality: the component must be attached on a GameObject to run lifecycle methods.
Concrete Example
Create PlayerController, attach to a Cube, press Play, and see Start run once. That confirms the script attached and lifecycle callbacks are active.
Key Takeaway
Recognize the skeleton so you can add variables and logic in the correct places without breaking Unity's expectations.
Try This
Rename the class to match the file name. If they mismatch, Unity may show a compile error and the script won't attach correctly.

screens.title: using Directives and UnityEngine
screens.narratorSegment: using directives are small statements that make types from another namespace available with short names. In Unity scripts you'll commonly see a using directive for UnityEngine, and sometimes for System. Collections or System. Collections. Generic. UnityEngine provides essential types like GameObject, Transform, Vector3, and MonoBehaviour itself. When you see a using directive at the top of a file it simply means the compiler can resolve those type names without you typing a full namespace path each time. A concrete example: with UnityEngine included you can write GameObject or Transform directly instead of a longer fully qualified path. A common misconception is that removing a using directive changes runtime behavior; it only affects whether the compiler recognizes unqualified type names. If the directive is missing, you must either add it or reference the full namespace. Understanding namespacing keeps your code readable and prevents compile errors when refactoring or moving code between projects. This small detail helps you write clearer scripts and improves collaboration, because teammates will expect consistent use of common Unity namespaces. using Directives and UnityEngine means using directives import sets of types so you can reference them concisely; unityengine is required to access core engine types.. In practical terms, why namespaces like unityengine matter for scripts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › using Directives
Definition

What are using directives?

They let the compiler resolve type names from a namespace without requiring fully qualified names. UnityEngine is the core namespace for the engine's types and services.

using System.Collections;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;
Concrete Benefits
  • Simpler code: write Transform instead of a long path.
  • Fewer errors: the compiler recognizes common engine types.
  • Clear intent: other developers see which libraries you rely on.
Misconception: Removing a using directive changes behavior. It only affects compilation names; runtime behavior is unchanged if references are resolved.

screens.title: MonoBehaviour and Attaching Scripts to GameObjects
screens.narratorSegment: MonoBehaviour is the bridge between your C# code and Unity's runtime. When a class inherits from MonoBehaviour it gains the ability to be added as a component to a GameObject in the scene. That attachment is what causes Unity to call special methods like Awake, Start, and Update at the appropriate times. Think of GameObjects as containers and MonoBehaviours as attachable behavior modules. A practical example: creating a PlayerController class that inherits from MonoBehaviour and dragging it onto a Cube makes that Cube carry the behaviors defined in the script. If your class does not inherit from MonoBehaviour, it will not appear in the Add Component menu and cannot receive lifecycle callbacks. This difference is often confused with general C# inheritance. The architecture matters when designing systems: keep data-only classes separate from components that require Unity callbacks. Using MonoBehaviour where needed lets Unity manage the component lifecycle; using plain classes for data reduces overhead and simplifies unit testing. This distinction helps you design cleaner projects and prevents common attachment errors when scripts fail to show up in the Inspector. MonoBehaviour and Attaching Scripts to GameObjects means inheritance from monobehaviour makes your class a component that can be attached to gameobjects and participate in unity's lifecycle.. In practical terms, how inheritance enables component behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Concept

MonoBehaviour as a bridge

Inheriting from MonoBehaviour lets Unity treat the class as a component, enabling Inspector display and lifecycle callbacks.

Design tip: separate data classes from components. Use plain classes for pure data, MonoBehaviour for things that need engine callbacks.
Attach Flow
Create script
PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
Drag to GameObject

Runtime

screens.title: Awake() vs Start()
screens.narratorSegment: Awake and Start are both initialization callbacks, but they have different guarantees and ideal uses. Awake is called when the script instance is being loaded. It runs even if the component is disabled and it always runs before any Start calls. This makes Awake the right place to initialize internal state and set up references that other scripts might depend on. Start is called before the first frame update but only if the component is enabled. Start is ideal for one-time setup that assumes all Awake calls have completed, such as initializing behavior that relies on other objects' Awake initialization. A concrete example: if you need to cache a reference to a component on the same GameObject, Awake is safe; if you must reference something that other objects initialize in Awake, delay that work to Start. A frequent mistake is placing dependency code in Start when the dependency isn't ready; this causes null references or race conditions. Another misconception is expecting Awake to run after Start — the order is always Awake first, then Start. Reflect on this: choose Awake for early internal setup and Start for actions that require other objects to be initialized.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Awake vs Start
Definition

Awake

Called when the script instance is loaded. Runs before Start on all objects and executes whether the component is enabled or not. Use for early initialization.

Example: cache internal references to components on the same GameObject so other scripts can rely on those references in Start.
Definition

Start

Called once before the first frame update, only if the component is enabled. Use Start for initialization that depends on other objects' Awake methods having completed.

Common mistake: placing dependency setup in Start when that dependency is initialized later. Prefer Awake for binding your own internal components.
Check Your Understanding
If two objects both use Awake and Start, Awake runs on all objects first, then Start runs on all enabled objects.
Analogy
Think of Awake as loading the actors and Start as telling them to begin the scene once everyone is on stage.
Key Takeaway
Choose Awake for guaranteed early setup; choose Start when initialization requires other objects to be ready.

screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and Access Modifiers
screens.narratorSegment: Variables are named storage slots in your script and every variable in C# has a data type that determines what values it can hold. Common types you'll use in Unity include int for whole numbers, float for decimal numbers, and string for text. When you declare a variable you also choose an access modifier such as public or private. Public variables appear in the Unity Inspector, letting designers and you adjust values without changing code; private variables are internal to the script. A concrete example is public float moveSpeed = 5.0f; which declares a floating-point variable exposed to the Inspector with an initial value. The f suffix denotes a float literal. A common misconception is that making everything public is safe; overexposing variables can break encapsulation and make debugging harder. Instead, expose only those variables you intend to tune externally and keep internal state private. Use comments to document purpose and consider serialized private fields when you want Inspector exposure without public access. Understanding variables and types helps you control memory, prevent type mismatches, and make your scripts easier to maintain and tune in the Editor.

keyIdea.title: Variables Matter
keyIdea.text: Use typed variables to store values. Use public to expose tunable parameters in the Inspector while keeping internal state private.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Variables & Types
Core Concept

Typed variables

public float moveSpeed = 5.0f; // exposed in Inspector
private int currentLives = 3;     // internal state
[SerializeField]
private string playerName = "Hero"; // visible in Inspector but not public
Use public for designer-tunable values. Use SerializeField to keep a field private but still show it in the Inspector when needed.
Why it matters
Proper typing prevents runtime surprises and makes the Inspector a powerful tuning surface for designers and rapid prototyping.
Misconception
Making every field public is convenient but leads to maintenance problems. Prefer minimal exposure.
Example
Set moveSpeed in the Inspector while testing to tune movement without recompiling code.

screens.title: Expose Variables to the Inspector and Debug with Debug.Log
screens.narratorSegment: Exposing variables to the Inspector and using Debug. Log are two fast feedback techniques that speed iteration. When you mark a field public it appears in the Inspector where you can change the value between runs. For example, public float moveSpeed = 5.0f; lets you tune movement speed without editing code. Debug. Log allows you to print messages to Unity's Console at runtime. Place a Debug. Log call in Start to verify initialization, for example printing the current value of moveSpeed. A concrete scenario: attach PlayerController to a Cube, set moveSpeed to 7 in the Inspector, press Play, and check the Console to see the printed message. That confirms the runtime value and that Start executed. A common mistake is expecting Debug. Log messages to appear without opening the Console window; always open the Console to view output. Overusing Debug. Log can clutter the Console; prefer concise messages and remove or gate verbose logging once you confirm behavior. Combined, Inspector tuning and Console checks give you a reliable loop: change values, run, observe, and iterate quickly. In practical terms, use public fields and console output to observe runtime state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Script Attachment and Console Output
screens.narratorSegment: When a script doesn't behave as expected, a few common issues usually explain the problem. First, compile errors prevent scripts from running. Unity stops code execution when compilation fails. Always open the Console and resolve the first compile-time error; subsequent errors may be a cascade. Second, scripts must be attached to a GameObject to receive lifecycle callbacks. If Awake or Start doesn't run, confirm the component is on a GameObject and that the component is enabled. Third, the class name must match the file name for MonoBehaviour components to be recognized and attached correctly; renaming the class without renaming the file will cause Unity to treat them as mismatched and may produce a compile error. Fourth, Debug. Log output can be missed if the Console's filters hide log types, or if you haven't opened the Console window at all. A quick checklist: fix compile errors, confirm attachment and enabled state, match file and class names, and open Console with appropriate filters. This routine helps you recover quickly and keeps development momentum while you iterate on gameplay behaviors. screens.title: Design Guidance: Public vs Private and SerializeField
screens.narratorSegment: As you develop scripts, prefer exposing only the fields that designers must tune. Public fields are convenient because they appear in the Inspector, but they also create wide access from other scripts which can complicate maintenance. A balanced approach uses private fields for internal state and SerializeField when you want Inspector visibility without making a field public. For example, [SerializeField] private int maxHealth = 5; shows in the Inspector but prevents other classes from changing it directly. Document fields with comments so teammates understand why a value is exposed. Another practical tip: give default values in code so the script behaves predictably even before the Inspector is tuned. A common misconception is that Inspector values always override code defaults; Inspector-assigned values persist on the component and replace defaults when the component is first created. When you reset a component, defaults from code are reapplied. These practices promote clear APIs for your components, safer refactoring, and easier collaboration between programmers and designers. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn how C# scripts plug into Unity, why Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code is the recommended editor, and how the MonoBehaviour lifecycle drives script execution. We'll walk through configuring your external script editor inside Unity preferences so you gain features like code completion and debugging. Then you'll open a generated script, identify the using directives, class declaration, and example lifecycle methods. You'll add a simple public variable so it shows in the Inspector, attach the script to a 3D object, and press Play to confirm Awake and Start messages appear in the Console. This foundation matters because it turns static scenes into interactive behaviors and gives you the tools to inspect and fix runtime problems quickly. A common misconception is that a script automatically runs without being attached; it must be a component on a GameObject to trigger lifecycle callbacks. As you progress, these basics will let you prototype movement, interactions, and game state reliably. Keep an eye on the Console for Debug. Log messages; they are your first diagnostics. Ready to start exploring the topics and step-by-step exercises that follow?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure Unity to use Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code as the external C# editor, create and inspect a basic C# script, and attach it to a GameObject so it executes. You will understand the main syntax elements: using directives, class declarations, variables with explicit data types, and comments. You will be able to expose public variables to the Inspector for rapid tuning and use the Console to observe Debug. Log output. Finally, you'll know when to use Awake versus Start for initialization and how that affects dependencies between objects. Each objective links practical steps to why they matter: editor configuration unlocks IntelliSense and debugging which speeds development; knowing script structure prevents common attachment mistakes; and correctly timed initialization prevents race conditions between objects. These skills let you move from static scenes to interactive prototypes quickly, and they form the foundation for movement, input handling, and component interactions you'll learn next.

This screen expands the objectives into verifiable steps you can perform. You'll create a project and a simple script, attach it to a 3D object, and confirm Console output from both Awake and Start. You will also edit a public variable, change it in the Inspector, and run again to see the updated value printed. These checks are important because they prove both script attachment and Inspector exposure are working. We'll also highlight common pitfalls, such as forgetting to attach the script, disabling the component, or mis-typing a variable so its default value does not appear. As you practice, compare Awake and Start: use Awake to set up references that other Start methods may need, and use Start for one-time actions that depend on other objects being ready. Completing these actions gives you a short checklist to move forward with movement, input, and more advanced scripting patterns.

Configuring Unity to use Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code as the external script editor is a small step that yields big productivity gains. Begin by opening Unity, then open Edit, Preferences, and the External Tools section. There you will select Visual Studio or V S Code as the External Script Editor. This connection gives you code completion, symbol lookup, and the ability to attach the debugger to a running Unity editor. A concrete example: when you open a C# script from the Project window, Visual Studio will show method suggestions and automatically jump to definitions, which saves time versus searching manually. A common misconception is that any editor will behave the same with Unity; in practice, the integrated tooling the IDE provides is the difference between slow trial-and-error and fast iterative debugging. If your scripts don't open in the selected editor, check the package installation and confirm Unity was restarted after installing Visual Studio components. Finally, test your setup by creating a simple script, opening it, and verifying that IntelliSense suggests types like GameObject and MonoBehaviour and that breakpoints hit when you attach the debugger. This verification closes the loop and ensures your development environment is ready for rapid scripting.

A freshly created C# script in Unity follows a predictable skeleton that helps Unity wire your code into the engine. At the top you will see using directives. These are short statements that allow your code to reference namespaces that contain types and utilities. For Unity development, UnityEngine is the essential namespace because it holds GameObject, Transform, and many engine services. Below that you find a class declaration. The typical form declares a public class that inherits from MonoBehaviour. Inheritance from MonoBehaviour is what enables the script to be attached to a GameObject as a component and to receive lifecycle callbacks from Unity. Inside the class you will initially see methods like Start and Update. Start runs once before the first frame update if the component is enabled, and Update runs every frame. Many learners assume methods in a script run automatically even if the script is not attached; that is a misconception. A class that does not inherit from MonoBehaviour cannot be added as a component. A concrete example is creating PlayerController : MonoBehaviour and observing that after you attach it to a Cube, the Start method runs and prints a message. Understanding this structure prevents common errors and sets you up to add variables and behaviors safely.

using directives are small statements that make types from another namespace available with short names. In Unity scripts you'll commonly see a using directive for UnityEngine, and sometimes for System. Collections or System. Collections. Generic. UnityEngine provides essential types like GameObject, Transform, Vector3, and MonoBehaviour itself. When you see a using directive at the top of a file it simply means the compiler can resolve those type names without you typing a full namespace path each time. A concrete example: with UnityEngine included you can write GameObject or Transform directly instead of a longer fully qualified path. A common misconception is that removing a using directive changes runtime behavior; it only affects whether the compiler recognizes unqualified type names. If the directive is missing, you must either add it or reference the full namespace. Understanding namespacing keeps your code readable and prevents compile errors when refactoring or moving code between projects. This small detail helps you write clearer scripts and improves collaboration, because teammates will expect consistent use of common Unity namespaces. using Directives and UnityEngine means using directives import sets of types so you can reference them concisely; unityengine is required to access core engine types.. In practical terms, why namespaces like unityengine matter for scripts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

MonoBehaviour is the bridge between your C# code and Unity's runtime. When a class inherits from MonoBehaviour it gains the ability to be added as a component to a GameObject in the scene. That attachment is what causes Unity to call special methods like Awake, Start, and Update at the appropriate times. Think of GameObjects as containers and MonoBehaviours as attachable behavior modules. A practical example: creating a PlayerController class that inherits from MonoBehaviour and dragging it onto a Cube makes that Cube carry the behaviors defined in the script. If your class does not inherit from MonoBehaviour, it will not appear in the Add Component menu and cannot receive lifecycle callbacks. This difference is often confused with general C# inheritance. The architecture matters when designing systems: keep data-only classes separate from components that require Unity callbacks. Using MonoBehaviour where needed lets Unity manage the component lifecycle; using plain classes for data reduces overhead and simplifies unit testing. This distinction helps you design cleaner projects and prevents common attachment errors when scripts fail to show up in the Inspector. In practical terms, how inheritance enables component behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Awake and Start are both initialization callbacks, but they have different guarantees and ideal uses. Awake is called when the script instance is being loaded. It runs even if the component is disabled and it always runs before any Start calls. This makes Awake the right place to initialize internal state and set up references that other scripts might depend on. Start is called before the first frame update but only if the component is enabled. Start is ideal for one-time setup that assumes all Awake calls have completed, such as initializing behavior that relies on other objects' Awake initialization. A concrete example: if you need to cache a reference to a component on the same GameObject, Awake is safe; if you must reference something that other objects initialize in Awake, delay that work to Start. A frequent mistake is placing dependency code in Start when the dependency isn't ready; this causes null references or race conditions. Another misconception is expecting Awake to run after Start — the order is always Awake first, then Start. Reflect on this: choose Awake for early internal setup and Start for actions that require other objects to be initialized.

Variables are named storage slots in your script and every variable in C# has a data type that determines what values it can hold. Common types you'll use in Unity include int for whole numbers, float for decimal numbers, and string for text. When you declare a variable you also choose an access modifier such as public or private. Public variables appear in the Unity Inspector, letting designers and you adjust values without changing code; private variables are internal to the script. A concrete example is public float moveSpeed = 5.0f; which declares a floating-point variable exposed to the Inspector with an initial value. The f suffix denotes a float literal. A common misconception is that making everything public is safe; overexposing variables can break encapsulation and make debugging harder. Instead, expose only those variables you intend to tune externally and keep internal state private. Use comments to document purpose and consider serialized private fields when you want Inspector exposure without public access. Understanding variables and types helps you control memory, prevent type mismatches, and make your scripts easier to maintain and tune in the Editor.

Exposing variables to the Inspector and using Debug. Log are two fast feedback techniques that speed iteration. When you mark a field public it appears in the Inspector where you can change the value between runs. For example, public float moveSpeed = 5.0f; lets you tune movement speed without editing code. Debug. Log allows you to print messages to Unity's Console at runtime. Place a Debug. Log call in Start to verify initialization, for example printing the current value of moveSpeed. A concrete scenario: attach PlayerController to a Cube, set moveSpeed to 7 in the Inspector, press Play, and check the Console to see the printed message. That confirms the runtime value and that Start executed. A common mistake is expecting Debug. Log messages to appear without opening the Console window; always open the Console to view output. Overusing Debug. Log can clutter the Console; prefer concise messages and remove or gate verbose logging once you confirm behavior. Combined, Inspector tuning and Console checks give you a reliable loop: change values, run, observe, and iterate quickly. Attaching a script to a GameObject is a straightforward action that connects your code to the scene. Start by creating a 3D object, such as a Cube, in the Hierarchy. Then create a new C# script in the Project window and give it a descriptive name like GreetingScript or PlayerController. Drag that script onto the Cube in the Hierarchy or onto the Inspector for the selected GameObject. Once attached, the script appears as a component in the Inspector where public fields are visible. Press Play to run the scene. Open the Console via Window, General, Console to observe messages. If you placed Debug. Log statements in Awake and Start, you will see Awake messages first, then Start messages. A common pitfall is forgetting to press Play after attaching the script; attaching alone does not run lifecycle methods. Another mistake is renaming the class without renaming the file; Unity expects the class name to match the file name for components. Finally, if the Console shows errors, fix compile-time errors before expecting lifecycle callbacks. Observing Awake and Start messages proves the script is attached, compiles, and runs as part of the active scene.

When a script doesn't behave as expected, a few common issues usually explain the problem. First, compile errors prevent scripts from running. Unity stops code execution when compilation fails. Always open the Console and resolve the first compile-time error; subsequent errors may be a cascade. Second, scripts must be attached to a GameObject to receive lifecycle callbacks. If Awake or Start doesn't run, confirm the component is on a GameObject and that the component is enabled. Third, the class name must match the file name for MonoBehaviour components to be recognized and attached correctly; renaming the class without renaming the file will cause Unity to treat them as mismatched and may produce a compile error. Fourth, Debug. Log output can be missed if the Console's filters hide log types, or if you haven't opened the Console window at all. A quick checklist: fix compile errors, confirm attachment and enabled state, match file and class names, and open Console with appropriate filters. This routine helps you recover quickly and keeps development momentum while you iterate on gameplay behaviors. As you develop scripts, prefer exposing only the fields that designers must tune. Public fields are convenient because they appear in the Inspector, but they also create wide access from other scripts which can complicate maintenance. A balanced approach uses private fields for internal state and SerializeField when you want Inspector visibility without making a field public. For example, [SerializeField] private int maxHealth = 5; shows in the Inspector but prevents other classes from changing it directly. Document fields with comments so teammates understand why a value is exposed. Another practical tip: give default values in code so the script behaves predictably even before the Inspector is tuned. A common misconception is that Inspector values always override code defaults; Inspector-assigned values persist on the component and replace defaults when the component is first created. When you reset a component, defaults from code are reapplied. These practices promote clear APIs for your components, safer refactoring, and easier collaboration between programmers and designers. This structure determines how Unity calls your code at runtime. Third, use typed variables and access modifiers carefully: declare floats, ints, and strings with sensible defaults, expose only the parameters you need in the Inspector, and use Debug. Log to confirm runtime behavior. Together, these practices let you attach scripts to GameObjects, tune behavior in the Editor, and verify execution with the Console.
